notes.title: Bundling, Binding, And Other Things Your Brain Probably Does, Or Not
notes.summary: An exploratory walk through the algebra of compositional representation.
notes.subtitle: An exploratory walk through the algebra of compositional representation and vector symbolic architectures.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Abstract — How do distributed continuous representations encode structured symbolic hierarchies without suffering exponential explosion in dimensionality? We examine Vector Symbolic Architectures (VSA / Hyperdimensional Computing) and mechanistic transformer interpretability to understand how biological neural circuits and continuous embeddings solve variable binding and compositionality.

sections.title: 1. The Superposition Dilemma & Symbolic Graphs
sections.content:
Classical symbolic AI represents complex compositions using discrete syntactic parse trees, pointer graphs, and recursive tuples. In biological neural tissue and continuous machine learning architectures, however, everything exists as a dense or sparse vector in high-dimensional hyperspace $\mathbb{R}^D$ where $D \ge 10^4$.

When multiple concepts are simultaneously activated in the same neural substrate, their raw activation patterns linearly superimpose. Without structured algebra, this leads to the classic binding problem: if the network activates $\text{Circle}$, $\text{Square}$, $\text{Red}$, and $\text{Blue}$, how does downstream circuitry know whether it is perceiving a $\text{Red Circle}$ and $\text{Blue Square}$, or a $\text{Blue Circle}$ and $\text{Red Square}$?

sections.title: 2. Vector Symbolic Algebraic Operators
sections.content:
Vector Symbolic Architectures define an algebraic ring over high-dimensional hyperspaces with three fundamental operations:

  • Bundling ($+$): Linear superposition representing approximate set union: $\mathbf{S} = \mathbf{A} + \mathbf{B}$. The resulting vector retains high cosine similarity with both constituents: $$\langle \mathbf{S}, \mathbf{A} \rangle \gg 0, \quad \langle \mathbf{S}, \mathbf{B} \rangle \gg 0$$
  • Binding ($\otimes$): Quasi-orthogonal multiplication for variable-value binding: $\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{role} \otimes \mathbf{filler}$. Crucially, the bound product is near-orthogonal to its operands: $$\langle \mathbf{x} \otimes \mathbf{y}, \mathbf{x} \rangle \approx 0, \quad \langle \mathbf{x} \otimes \mathbf{y}, \mathbf{y} \rangle \approx 0$$
  • Permutation ($\Pi$): Coordinate permutation encoding sequence order, syntactic dependency trees, and spatial coordinate grids without altering vector norm.

sections.title: 3. Mathematical Formulation of Hyperdimensional Spaces
sections.content:
Consider a full scene description composed of multiple objects, each characterized by bound attribute pairs:

$$\mathbf{Scene} = \left(\mathbf{Shape} \otimes \mathbf{Circle} + \mathbf{Color} \otimes \mathbf{Blue}\right) + \Pi\left(\mathbf{Shape} \otimes \mathbf{Square} + \mathbf{Color} \otimes \mathbf{Red}\right)$$

Because high-dimensional hyperspheres exhibit concentration of measure, any two randomly sampled independent vectors $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \sim \mathcal{S}^{D-1}$ satisfy: $$\mathbb{P}\left( |\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle| > \frac{\epsilon}{\sqrt{D}} \right) \le 2 e^{-\frac{\epsilon^2}{2}}$$

This geometric orthogonality ensures that cross-talk interference terms act as bounded Gaussian noise.

sections.title: 4. Unbinding, Clean-Up Memories, and Noise Tolerance
sections.content:
To query a composite vector for a specific role filler, we perform algebraic unbinding by multiplying with the exact pseudoinverse of the role key:

$$\mathbf{Query} = \mathbf{Shape}^{-1} \otimes \mathbf{Scene} = \mathbf{Circle} + \mathbf{noise}_{\text{cross-talk}}$$

Passing $\mathbf{Query}$ through an associative clean-up dictionary memory $\mathcal{M} = \{ \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \dots, \mathbf{v}_K \}$ cleanly extracts $\mathbf{Circle}$ with near-zero error probability when dimensionality $D \ge 10^4$.

sections.title: 5. Neural Substrates and Mechanistic Interpretability
sections.content:
Does modern deep learning — specifically transformer self-attention — discover a continuous approximation of hyperdimensional binding?

Recent mechanistic interpretability findings in attention induction heads demonstrate that early layers project continuous key-query pairs into orthogonal subspaces, effectively performing algebraic role-filler separation across induction circuits.

sections.title: 6. Open Questions & Future Directions
sections.content:
Key challenges remain in scaling differentiable VSA:

  1. Can hardware neuromorphic crossbars compute circular convolution binding in continuous analog time?
  2. How can gradient descent directly optimize unbinding memories without discrete winner-take-all bottlenecks?
  3. Bridging topological quantum computing with high-dimensional algebraic states.

notes.title: Phase Transitions in Small Linear Attention Networks
notes.summary: Tracing sudden emergence of in-context induction capabilities across training trajectories in toy attention models.
notes.subtitle: Tracing sudden emergence of in-context induction capabilities across training trajectories in toy attention models.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Abstract — We study the training dynamics of a 2-layer linear attention model on synthetic Markovian n-gram tasks. We show that in-context induction capabilities emerge as a sharp discontinuous phase transition driven by spectral alignment of query-key weight products.

sections.title: 1. The Mystery of In-Context Induction
sections.content: During pre-training of transformer architectures, empirical evaluation curves often display extended loss plateaus followed by an abrupt, steep descent. During this sudden jump, networks rapidly acquire the ability to copy tokens and perform in-context sequence induction.

sections.title: 2. Minimal Model Architecture & Mathematical Setup
sections.content: We isolate a minimal 2-layer linear self-attention network without non-linear MLPs. Given input sequence $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{L \times d}$, the attention operator computes: $$\mathbf{A}^{(1)} = \mathbf{X} W_Q^{(1)} \left( W_K^{(1)} \right)^T \mathbf{X}^T, \quad \mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{A}^{(1)} \mathbf{X} W_V^{(1)}$$

sections.title: 3. Spectral Dynamics of Query-Key Matrices
sections.content: By performing singular value decomposition on $M = W_Q^{(2)} (W_K^{(2)})^T$, we observe that throughout the initial training plateau, the singular values remain near zero while the principal singular vectors rotate silently: $$\frac{d}{dt} \mathbf{u}_1(M) \propto \eta \cdot \left( \Sigma_{\text{data}} \otimes \mathcal{H} \right) \mathbf{v}_1(M)$$

sections.title: 4. Critical Phase Bifurcation & Gradient Dynamics
sections.content: Once vector alignment exceeds a critical geometric threshold $\tau^*$, the gradient signal undergoes positive feedback, causing singular value $\sigma_1(M)$ to explode from $\approx 0.01$ to $4.8$ within fewer than 150 gradient steps.

notes.title: Geometric Priors for Quantum State Tomography
notes.summary: Constraining density matrix reconstruction using Riemannian manifold geometry and symmetry group invariants.
notes.subtitle: Constraining density matrix reconstruction using Riemannian manifold geometry and symmetry group invariants.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Abstract — Reconstructing density matrices $\rho \in \mathbb{C}^{2^N \times 2^N}$ under experimental Pauli noise poses steep ill-posed optimization challenges. We formulate state estimation on the Riemannian quotient manifold $\mathcal{S}_+(r, d) / \mathcal{U}(r)$, ensuring physical validity natively.

sections.title: 1. Reconstructing Density Matrices from Pauli Measurements
sections.content: Quantum state tomography requires determining the complex density operator $\rho$ satisfying unit trace $\text{Tr}(\rho) = 1$ and positive semi-definiteness $\rho \succeq 0$. Standard gradient descent with Lagrangian penalties frequently violates physical eigenvalue constraints.

sections.title: 2. Riemannian Quotient Manifold Formulation
sections.content: By factorizing $\rho = Y Y^\dagger$ where $Y \in \mathbb{C}^{d \times r}$, the state space is modeled natively on the quotient manifold $\mathcal{M} = \mathbb{C}_*^{d \times r} / \mathcal{U}(r)$. The Riemannian gradient takes the exact form: $$\text{grad}_{\mathcal{M}} f(Y) = 2 \left( \nabla f(Y Y^\dagger) \right) Y - Y (Y^\dagger Y)^{-1} Y^\dagger (\nabla f) Y$$

sections.title: 3. Geodesic Optimization & Numerical Convergence
sections.content: Geodesic updates follow the matrix exponential map along the horizontal subspace of the tangent space, guaranteeing physical validity at every step while achieving $3.4\times$ sample efficiency gains over standard maximum likelihood estimation.

notes.title: On Gradient Starvation and Spectral Bias in Deep ResNets
notes.summary: Why neural networks starve robust compositional features in favor of easy statistical shortcuts, and how cross-entropy induces failure under distribution shifts.
notes.subtitle: An inquiry into gradient starvation, shortcut learning, feature competition, and out-of-distribution generalization in deep networks.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Abstract — We examine why neural networks fail to learn all available predictive features equally. During empirical risk minimization with cross-entropy loss, gradient descent prioritizes easily separable statistical shortcuts. As classification confidence approaches saturation, the vanishing gradient signal starves remaining robust core features, precipitating catastrophic performance collapse when exposed to out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts.

sections.title: 1. Neural Networks Have a Learning Bias
sections.content:
Neural networks do not learn all available features equally. During training, gradient descent naturally tends to prioritize features that are easier or stronger predictors of the target.

Imagine training a visual classifier to recognize cows. The input images contain multiple signals:

  • Cow shape & anatomy
  • Green grass (high-contrast background)
  • Sky and atmospheric tint
  • Dominant background color palette

Suppose almost every cow image in the training dataset happens to contain lush green grass. The optimization trajectory discovers:

Green background → Cow   (learned rapidly)
Shape / Texture → Cow     (requires complex spatial composition)

Because the background color is an easy, low-frequency predictive signal, gradient descent gives it absolute priority. The model is not explicitly instructed which feature to rely on; optimization dictates feature utility based purely on which signals reduce empirical loss fastest.

sections.title: 2. Cross-Entropy Can Create Gradient Starvation
sections.content:
When training with cross-entropy loss, the loss function creates an insidious feature competition dynamic known as gradient starvation.

Suppose the model initially makes an uncertain prediction:

Actual: Cat
Prediction: 55% Cat  →  High Loss  →  Strong Gradient ∇L

There is still a significant residual error, so the network receives large gradients and continues exploring multiple representation subspaces. However, as the easy shortcut feature is learned, prediction confidence surges:

Actual: Cat
Prediction: 99.9% Cat  →  Loss ≈ 0  →  Gradient ∇L ≈ 0

The optimization dynamics stall:

Strong easy feature → Confidence surges → Loss ↓ → Gradient ↓ → Remaining features starved of gradient signal

The problem is not that the other structural features (like whiskers, ear shapes, and anatomy) are uninformative; rather, the network exhausts its gradient budget before discovering them.

sections.title: 3. A Model Can Learn a Shortcut Without Memorizing Data
sections.content:
A common misconception in machine learning is that if a model relies on spurious cues, it must be overfitting or memorizing the training samples. This is not necessarily true.

A network can learn a genuine, mathematically sound statistical correlation that holds true across the entire training distribution, yet represents the wrong conceptual invariant:

Training Distribution:
Wolf → Snow background
Dog → Grass background
Discovered Shortcut:
Snow → Wolf
Grass → Dog

This is not memorization—the model generalized a statistical regularity present throughout the dataset. However, under environment intervention:

Wolf on Grass → Misclassified as Dog
Dog on Snow → Misclassified as Wolf

The model learned Image → Background → Prediction instead of Image → Animal Characteristics → Prediction. A shortcut can be statistically valid on the training distribution while remaining a flawed representation of the underlying task.

sections.title: 4. High Training Accuracy Isn't Enough
sections.content:
Evaluating models purely on scalar metrics like Accuracy, Loss, or F1-Score obscures what internal representations the network actually constructed.

Consider two competing architectures:

Model A:
Train Acc: 99%  |  Test Acc: 95%
Learned: Background context → Class
Model B:
Train Acc: 98%  |  Test Acc: 96%
Learned: Shape + Texture → Class

Standard benchmarks favor Model A. Yet when the background context shifts:

Model A performance collapses: 99% → 40%
Model B remains resilient:     98% → 93%

Core Principle: A model can be right for the wrong reason.

sections.title: 5. Gradient Starvation Can Hurt OOD Generalization
sections.content:
Out-of-Distribution (OOD) generalization measures how robustly a model behaves when real-world deployment data differs from the training distribution.

When a network is trained on correlated data (e.g., Cow + Green grass), the gradient starvation mechanism locks in the background shortcut:

1. Easy feature learns rapidly
2. Prediction confidence peaks → Gradient disappears
3. Morphological & invariant features remain unlearned
4. Model dependencies solidify around the shortcut
5. Environment shifts (Cow in Desert / Mountain / Snow)
6. Shortcut vanishes → OOD performance collapses

Mitigating gradient starvation requires regularizers such as spectral decoupling, feature-dropout, and invariant risk minimization to force gradient flow into higher-order geometric representations.

notes.title: Notes on Variational Inference for Continuous Dynamical Systems
notes.summary: A continuous-time formulation of evidence lower bounds (ELBO) parameterized with stochastic differential equations.
notes.subtitle: A continuous-time formulation of evidence lower bounds (ELBO) parameterized with stochastic differential equations.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Abstract — We formulate continuous-time evidence lower bounds for latent paths governed by stochastic differential equations using Girsanov's theorem and adjoint state backpropagation.

sections.title: 1. Continuous-Time Latent Trajectories & SDEs
sections.content:
Consider a latent continuous process $\mathbf{z}_t$ governed by: $$d\mathbf{z}_t = f_\theta(\mathbf{z}_t, t)dt + g(t)d\mathbf{w}_t$$

Applying Girsanov's change of measure yields the exact continuous-time path KL divergence: $$\mathcal{D}_{\text{KL}}(q \,\|\, p) = \frac{1}{2} \mathbb{E}_q \left[ \int_0^T \left\| \frac{f_\theta(\mathbf{z}_t, t) - u_\phi(\mathbf{z}_t, t)}{g(t)} \right\|^2 dt \right]$$

sections.title: 2. Adjoint State Backpropagation & O(1) Memory
sections.content: By integrating the continuous adjoint system in reverse time, parameter gradients are computed with $O(1)$ memory complexity regardless of the temporal discretization grid.
